summary: Weekly POC sync to review quality evaluation results from last week's tests. Discussed scoring regressions for user-facing triage assistant, prompt-tuning steps, guardrail adjustments to reduce hallucinations, and plan for a canary rollout. Agreed on action items to update prompt set and run regression benchmarks. Security docs and pilot telemetry to be shared.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, we're on for 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Dr. Maya Patel: Maya here.
[00:07] Liam O'Connor: Liam, hi.
[00:09] Sofia Ruiz: Sofia here.
[00:11] Ethan Blake: Ethan.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Priya from Redwood, hey all.
[00:14] Alex Park: Alex from CS.
[00:16] Jordan Kim: Great. Quick agenda — we want to go over last week's quality eval, call out any regressions, discuss prompt changes and guardrail rules, then agree next steps. Priya, you want to kick off with the results?
[00:30] Priya Desai: Yep. So we ran the eval across the latest prompt set v1.3 and compared to the baseline v1.1. Overall accuracy on the structured triage outputs improved slightly, from 82% to 84%, but we saw an increase in hallucination rate for medication fields — small but notable, about 2.5% -> 5%.
[00:52] Ethan Blake: Hmm that medication spike is what we saw in production logs last Friday, right? The assistant started inventing dosages sometimes.
[01:00] Sofia Ruiz: Correct, and that's our main blocker for rolling to more clinics. We need guardrails there.
[01:05] Priya Desai: We dug into the examples — many are edge cases where the patient note mentions a past med in a historical context and the model attributes it to current meds. The prompt nudges helped previously, but the new phrasing to improve extraction of symptoms seemed to reduce context window for medications.
[01:25] Liam O'Connor: Can you share an example?
[01:27] Priya Desai: Sure — example 47 in the spreadsheet: "Patient denies current use of lisinopril, previously prescribed in 2016" — model pulled lisinopril as active and assigned dose 10mg.
[01:40] Dr. Maya Patel: That one I'm familiar with — it's a classic temporal reasoning issue.
[01:44] Jordan Kim: Ok, so cause looks like prompt tradeoff: optimizing symptom extraction hurt medication temporal parsing. Two paths: re-tune prompt to explicitly anchor med statements, or add a post-extraction guardrail that filters meds with 'historical' signals. Priya, which is quicker?
[02:02] Priya Desai: The guardrail is fastest — a rule-based heuristic to detect temporal cues and demote or null medication when historical context is present. Prompt rework will be iterative and needs regression tests.
[02:15] Ethan Blake: We can provide more examples of the historical phrasing to help tune heuristics.
[02:20] Priya Desai: Perfect. We already flagged 18 such examples; if you add 3-5 more, we can tune the heuristic this week.
[02:30] Sofia Ruiz: Timeline wise, we'd prefer a fix in the next sprint — so within two weeks ideally.
[02:36] Jordan Kim: Sounds reasonable. Now on scoring: we used a combined F1 + hallucination penalty metric. Priya, remind them how hallucination penalty is computed.
[02:45] Priya Desai: Sure. It's base F1 on extraction plus a -10 point penalty per hallucinated critical field (medication with dosage, allergy). The idea is to heavily punish confident but fabricated outputs. We're reporting normalized scores; baseline was 0.78 and current is 0.75 due to those meds.
[03:03] Liam O'Connor: That penalty helps, but I'm concerned about false positives on the penalty — when model is unsure it should abstain but still outputs something low confidence. Can we threshold confidence?
[03:14] Priya Desai: We're adding a confidence threshold that maps model token probabilities to a calibrated score; below threshold will result in 'unknown' which then triggers a fallback to human review. That reduced hallucinations in earlier runs.
[03:28] Dr. Maya Patel: Fallback to human review is OK but increases triage load — what's the expected percent increase?
[03:35] Priya Desai: In the tuned runs it's about 3-4% more human reviews, but the hallucination errors drop by ~60% in those groups. Tradeoff but safer for patient safety.
[03:46] Jordan Kim: Good notes. Next — regression detection. We ran automated regression tests across 2,500 prompts plus the curated edge set. We also did stratified sampling by specialty. There were a few regressions in cardiology notes. Priya, can you summarize root cause?
[04:02] Priya Desai: For cardiology, the sequences are longer and refer back to prior visits. We noticed the tokenizer truncation and the model's KV cache handling with longer sequences was causing context loss. That manifested as missing past procedures and occasionally swapping entities.
[04:20] Ethan Blake: Does that suggest we need a different model variant or longer context length?
[04:24] Priya Desai: Options: increase context window by switching to a model variant with longer context (cost up), or implement prefix caching for repeated patient history across requests — which Redwood's runtime supports via KV caching. For POC, prefix caching plus prompt restructuring is lower cost and quicker.
[04:40] Jordan Kim: Are there latency impacts with prefix caching?
[04:43] Priya Desai: Minimal at request time; it actually reduces per-request tokens in many cases. We measured tail latency unchanged within noise.
[04:50] Sofia Ruiz: Okay good. On guardrails — besides temporal med heuristic, any other rules recommended?
[04:55] Priya Desai: Yes — 1) explicit abstention triggers for low confidence, 2) regex checks for invalid dosages (e.g., 0.1 mg where normal is integer), 3) a denial list for hallucinated drug names that we've never seen in corpus, and 4) structured output validation (schema checks).
[05:12] Liam O'Connor: The regex for dosages might be brittle across international formats — we have some clinics that use commas.
[05:20] Priya Desai: Good point — we'll parameterize dose parsing per locale; Jordan will add that to action items.
[05:26] Jordan Kim: Noted. Now artifacts — we've shared a spreadsheet with the eval runs and prompt sets. Jordan, any notes on the prompts you changed last week?
[05:36] Jordan Kim: I moved from an inference style "extract current meds" to a more constrained instruction set with explicit examples and a final confirm step, but that tightened symptom extraction while exposing med temporal issues. We'll push a variant that keeps symptom instructions and adds med anchoring.
[05:50] Priya Desai: We'll call that prompt v1.3a and run side-by-side tests.
[05:54] Dr. Maya Patel: When you run side-by-side, can you include the scoring breakdown per field? We want to see meds, allergies, procedures separately.
[06:02] Priya Desai: Yes, the per-field breakdown is in the sheet but we'll make it more visible and add confidence buckets.
[06:09] Jordan Kim: On security and compliance, Liam asked last time about audit logs and retention. Alex, did you have the items to share?
[06:16] Alex Park: Yes — we sent SOC2 Type II summary and the security appendix link to your procurement alias last week. I'll re-share the direct links after the call and include the retention policy options (30/90/365 days) and KMS integration notes for customer-managed keys.
[06:31] Liam O'Connor: Great — also, do you support VPC private deployment as part of this POC if we need it later?
[06:37] Jordan Kim: We do — Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages; for the POC we started on hosted, but if you need private we can scope that as a next phase. It will add multi-week setup for networking and keys.
[06:50] Sofia Ruiz: Cost implications?
[06:52] Jordan Kim: Dedicated/reserved capacity increases baseline cost but gives predictable throughput; private adds infra and licensing. We'll model numbers if you want to explore.
[06:59] Dr. Maya Patel: Not yet — first stabilize quality.
[07:03] Priya Desai: Back to bench plan: priorities this week are guardrail heuristic for historical meds, prompt v1.3a run, and regression bench across cardiology edge set. We'll tag those in the sheet.
[07:15] Ethan Blake: We'll upload 3 additional edge-case transcripts by Wednesday.
[07:19] Jordan Kim: Great. Any questions on evaluation methodology?
[07:22] Liam O'Connor: One — how are you calibrating confidence to precision? We saw some cases where model confidence was high but wrong.
[07:30] Priya Desai: We recalibrate using Platt scaling over a validation split; also use softmax temperature tuning. We log per-token prob distributions to trace confident hallucinations.
[07:40] Ethan Blake: Can you show an example of the probability trace?
[07:43] Priya Desai: We'll attach a sample trace in the spreadsheet — it's noisy but helps.
[07:48] Jordan Kim: Ok shifting to rollout plan: once guardrails and prompt v1.3a pass regression, propose a canary with 5% traffic for one week, monitor hallucination rate, latency, and human review load. If stable, increase to 20%. Any objections?
[08:05] Dr. Maya Patel: Sounds sensible. Please include rollback thresholds — e.g., >2x hallucination or >10% human review increase.
[08:13] Jordan Kim: Noted. Priya, will you set thresholds?
[08:15] Priya Desai: Yes — we'll propose thresholds and share in the runbook.
[08:19] Sofia Ruiz: Also need SLA notes — what happens during a degradation window?
[08:23] Alex Park: We'll include the failover to previous model variant and canary abort playbook in the runbook.
[08:30] Liam O'Connor: One operational question — do we get token-level cost breakdowns for the canary so we can evaluate cost-per-interaction?
[08:37] Jordan Kim: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route token breakdowns and cost. We'll include sample dashboards for the canary.
[08:44] Priya Desai: Quick callouts from the eval: 1) hallucination penalty helped highlight meds, 2) prompt tweak improved symptom extraction (voice of user), 3) side-effect was med temporal regressions, 4) prefix caching likely fixes long context card issues.
[08:59] Ethan Blake: For prefix caching, what's the implementation overhead on our side?
[09:03] Priya Desai: Minimal — you send a patient-history key on requests and Redwood will attach cached prefix for subsequent calls. We can demo code snippets.
[09:12] Jordan Kim: We'll include a sample snippet in the follow-up email.
[09:15] Sofia Ruiz: On metrics, can we get more granular false positive labeling? Our product owner needs to see by severity.
[09:22] Priya Desai: Yes, we'll add severity tiers (critical, major, minor) into the eval sheet and map actions.
[09:29] Dr. Maya Patel: Critical is hallucinated med with dosage or allergy — those must be zero tolerance ideally.
[09:35] Jordan Kim: Agreed zero tolerance for critical, but operationally we will aim to reach a near-zero rate before broad rollout.
[09:41] Liam O'Connor: Anything on model variant? Are we locked to the one you used in POC?
[09:46] Priya Desai: No — Redwood supports switching model variant and routing policies; for consistency in eval we kept model X-102, but we can trial X-128 (longer context) for cardiology if needed.
[09:58] Ethan Blake: Please include cost delta for X-128 in the pricing appendix.
[10:02] Jordan Kim: Will do. Wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners. Jordan to share edited prompt set + eval scripts by Friday, Priya to run regression and share results next Monday, Ethan to upload edge-case transcripts Wednesday, Alex to re-share security links today. Any final questions?
[10:18] Sofia Ruiz: No, that's it.
[10:20] Jordan Kim: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with runbook and updated sheet.
[10:24] Dr. Maya Patel: Thanks all.
[10:25] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript contains imperfect transcription artifacts (e.g., occasional run-ons). References: shared spreadsheet "starlight-poc-eval-v1.xlsx" (link in CRM), sample code snippet for prefix caching will be attached, SOC2 appendix link to be re-shared.
